item.title: The Power of a Believable Story
item.description: A story can change expectations, draw in resources, and help create the reality it describes. That gives its author power, but it doesn't exempt the story from being tested.
item.content:encoded:
Late one night, I was in my study, headphones on, listening to a podcast by investors abroad. They were discussing Anthropic's valuation.

I opened Excel almost without thinking. Revenue growth, profit margins, terminal multiples, discount rates: I filled in the cells, made the assumptions more optimistic, then more optimistic again. However far I pushed them, the result was still a long way from $2 trillion.

Just as I was ready to dismiss the valuation, the host changed tack. On a strictly financial calculation, he said, $2 trillion was hard to defend. But the company had brought together some of the smartest people in the world, people with ability and ambition. They might produce something that changed everything. Seen that way, perhaps $2 trillion wasn't so unreasonable.

There wasn't a new number in that argument. No revised model. No additional cash-flow forecast. Yet I'd gone from shaking my head to nodding.

Only after closing the laptop did I notice what had happened. The calculation hadn't convinced me. A story had.

Soros's idea of reflexivity suggests a way to understand this: people use narratives to make sense of the world, and the actions they take on that basis change the world. That's my interpretation, not a quotation from him. That night, it stopped sounding like an elegant observation and began to feel like a practical problem.

Here's the uncomfortable argument I want to make. We don't always calculate first and believe afterward. Often we use a story to understand what is happening and form expectations, then find the logic and data that explain our choices. Expectations lead to action. Action changes conditions, and those changes can lend the story credibility. Follow that process far enough and you reach power: the ability to make a narrative believable can become the ability to influence prices and direct other people's actions.

1. Every valuation contains a story

The figures need some care. In its May 28, 2026 financing announcement, Anthropic disclosed a post-money valuation of $965 billion for its Series H round. An August report in the Financial Times described investors expecting an IPO valuation of $2 trillion or more and a year-end annualized revenue run rate of $100 billion to $120 billion, compared with roughly $47 billion in May. The IPO valuation and year-end figures were investor expectations at the time. A revenue run rate extrapolates recent performance; it isn't realized full-year revenue. Neither figure should be mistaken for a completed offering price or an achieved annual result. The timetable and final price remain subject to formal disclosure.

As someone who studies economics, I'm less interested here in settling what the company is worth than in a different question. Why can a valuation resist our calculations and still seem plausible?

Because every input in the model contains an account of the future. A growth rate puts a number on how quickly you expect AI to spread through the economy. A discount rate expresses your view of uncertainty. In the discounted cash-flow valuation of a fast-growing company, terminal value often makes up much of the result. That value depends on what you think the company will eventually become. Change the story and the model produces a different number.

I'd put it this strongly: a DCF can give a story a mathematical stamp of approval. Reason hasn't disappeared. Its inputs may already have been chosen by the narrative.

2. Belief can move resources

Many investors acknowledge narratives but file them under sentiment, as a layer of atmosphere surrounding the real valuation. I think that understates their effect.

In Narrative Economics, Robert Shiller examines how stories spread and influence economic decisions. Soros's reflexivity approaches a related problem from the other direction: participants' beliefs can change markets, and market outcomes can change those beliefs.

Put those ideas together and a feedback loop emerges. A narrative shapes expectations. Expectations help direct capital, talent, and attention. Those resources alter what is possible, and the results can become evidence for the original story.

Consider the claim that a company has assembled the smartest people in the world. Believing it can draw in more talented people, along with money and computing resources. That makes the company more likely to produce something valuable, which appears to confirm the initial claim. It becomes difficult to distinguish a prediction from an outcome the prediction helped bring about.

This is where narrative acquires pricing power. Someone who can define a convincing future can influence what others will pay for it today. At the extreme, belief in the company can command more value than its present patents or cash flows.

3. The story behind your own judgment

An obvious objection is that some stories are just hype, and a rational investor should be able to tell the difference.

But what makes you decide that one story is sensible and another absurd? Often it's a deeper narrative you haven't noticed yourself using.

Take Elon Musk's ambitions for flying cars and reusable rockets. Such proposals have attracted ridicule, frequently on the grounds that they have no practical use. Many objections deserve serious answers: energy consumption, noise, safety, regulation, and cost all matter.

Still, the judgment that something has no use may contain an assumption: useful means commercially viable now. That can feel like common sense, but it rests on a particular account of value, one grounded in cash flows already demonstrated. Another account places value on expanding what might become possible. Those positions answer different questions about what should count as valuable; neither wins merely by presenting itself as common sense.

Behavioral economists call one version of this problem the framing effect. Describe the same facts through a different frame and judgments can change. Someone ridiculing an idea may believe they stand outside the story, on the side of facts, while remaining inside an unexamined frame of their own.

My suspicion is that people who laugh at other people's narratives often haven't noticed the one they live in. Recognizing that doesn't require believing every pitch. It means laying out your own assumptions before judging someone else's.

4. How stories become wealth and political power

One way to turn a narrative into something tangible is through wealth. A persuasive account of the future can secure capital, talent, and time on better terms.

Another is through political power. Consider MAGA. I'm interested here in the mechanism rather than endorsing or opposing its politics. Elections also depend on institutions, social divisions, and the media environment. Within that broader picture, what role did those four letters play in the rise of a businessman with no previous public office to the presidency?

The narrative has a recognizable structure. A lost golden age gives discontent a history. A boundary between allies and opponents identifies who belongs and who is to blame. A promise of restoration turns present disappointment into a direction for action. Then a hat compresses the whole account into a cheap, wearable, recognizable symbol. Identifying with it requires very little explanation.

That structure suits a world with scarce attention. A detailed policy program won't reach everyone. Four letters can. They offer an explanation, a shared identity, and a destination.

Wealth gives people influence over where resources go. Political narratives can influence where people believe they should go. Power can work by making people want to move toward you, before an order is ever given.

5. What makes a story credible?

Stories are plentiful. Belief is harder to secure. I see at least four conditions that help explain the difference.

A story must be easy enough to retell; otherwise it won't travel beyond its first audience. It must point toward a future worth participating in. It needs something people can examine: a product, a financial statement, or visible progress. And the person telling it needs to have something at stake.

Three ideas help make sense of this.

A Schelling point is a focal point around which people can coordinate without communicating directly. A compelling story can play that role for strangers: if everyone else is looking in that direction, I'll look there too.

Signaling theory asks what makes a signal credible. Talk is cheap, so words alone tell us little. Costly actions can carry more information.

Skin in the game adds a question about consequences: how much does the speaker stand to lose?

Together, these ideas suggest why audiences often examine the storyteller's commitment as closely as the story. Has the founder committed their own savings and career? Have talented people put several precious years into the same undertaking? A large commitment can strengthen credibility, bring in followers, and increase the narrative's value.

What someone is willing to risk can matter as much as what they promise. The same ambitious sentence can carry very different weight depending on who says it.

6. Believing without surrendering judgment

This argument needs a limit. Otherwise it becomes a dangerous story of its own: tell a good enough tale and anything goes.

Narratives help determine who gets a chance to face reality. Without a convincing account of what you're doing, you may struggle to raise money, hire people, or obtain the time to experiment. In that sense, a story can buy admission. Once inside, the results still matter. Cash flows, working technology, customer retention, and an organization's ability to deliver cannot be supplied by a better pitch. A narrative can buy time, but it can't postpone delivery forever.

For investors, the question is whether the price contains a defensible premium for future possibility or a bubble sustained by belief. I return to three questions.

Who believes? Are the believers independent of one another, with different reasons and real money at stake, or are they repeating the same claims inside an echo chamber?

How long can they wait? A story that needs five years to unfold sits uneasily inside a price that demands proof within one. That mismatch is a risk even when the underlying idea is sound.

How much is at risk? What have the founders committed? What have their followers committed? And can your own position survive a long delay, or an outcome that never arrives?

Belief in a great story doesn't make every purchase price a good one. Much of the future may already be in the price. The company can succeed while the investment disappoints. These are questions for thinking about risk, not investment recommendations.

Before deciding how much you believe, ask who else believes, how long they can wait, and what each of you stands to lose.

Writing this brings me back to that late night in my study. I thought I was judging the world independently through Excel. I was also interpreting it through a story I'd grown used to telling myself.

What story is doing that work for you?

item.title: Finding Your Way Out, One Step at a Time
item.description: Protect your ability to keep going, recover your judgment, and rebuild your options. Getting out of a difficult situation takes more than betting everything on a comeback.
item.content:encoded:
The options you still have

Late one night in the autumn of 2021, I met Zhou in a private room at a Japanese restaurant in Beijing's Guomao district. There was a draft mortgage agreement on the table and an ashtray full of cigarette ends. A year earlier, his consumer-goods company had been valued at 500 million yuan, and investors had been queuing up to take him to dinner. Now a supply-chain failure and a downturn in his industry had left him with enough cash for half a month's payroll.

He wanted to borrow 5 million yuan to bridge the gap. "If I can just get through the Singles' Day sales, I can turn this around."

Debt reminders kept appearing on his phone. I looked at the punishing terms of the bridge loan and urged him to get professional advice about winding down the business before putting his family's last home at risk. He wouldn't hear it. Liquidation meant admitting defeat. He signed, pledged the house, and kept going. Six months later, the sales campaign had failed to rescue the business, the house was sold at auction, and he disappeared from our circle.

I've watched investors and founders lose money, and I've examined my own worst drawdowns. Zhou's experience wasn't an isolated one. People can suffer a similar loss of employment, business, or a relationship and emerge on very different timelines. One difference is the number of workable options they still possess. An economic way to understand a crisis is to look at the collapse of that choice set. A year before, Zhou could have raised capital, sold the business, or reduced its size. By holding on, he narrowed his options until only two ugly choices remained: borrow on ruinous terms and gamble, or go under immediately.

A bad decision produces a loss. The loss reduces your room to move. Anxiety then pushes you toward another bad decision. Adding more effort to an approach that has stopped working can strengthen that loop.

When income, confidence, capability, and outside conditions are all deteriorating, I wouldn't stake everything on one dramatic reversal. First stop the damage from feeding on itself. Then build a process in which small gains can accumulate. The work is to recover your options in the right order.

1. Stop the losses before attempting a comeback

The first objective is to stay in the game.

In investing, avoiding ruin takes precedence over any target return. A position down 50% might recover. If leverage forces you out and wipes out the capital, a later tenfold rally won't help. The same logic applies elsewhere. Continuing losses can consume every benefit of your next effort.

Start by examining cash flow, physical health, close family relationships, and the time you can still control. Put the numbers on paper. Cut spending maintained for appearances, stop businesses or side projects that keep losing money, and reduce avoidable sources of emotional strain. Under a zero-income scenario, how many months of basic living can your current resources cover?

Without a buffer, every decision becomes a forced trade. A shortage of money or time makes harsh terms and risky schemes look more attractive. Stopping a loss creates a period in which you don't have to decide under immediate pressure. The ability to correct a mistake may be the most valuable resource you have left.

During the venture-capital winter of 2018, a founder I knew was losing 400,000 yuan a month. Closing the company felt humiliating, so he mortgaged his property to keep paying salaries while waiting for another funding round. Six months later, the company failed, leaving him with personal liabilities of several million yuan and a place on a court's judgment-defaulter list. Another founder, facing six months of remaining cash, cut 80% of the operation and workforce, left an expensive office, and brought monthly spending below 30,000 yuan. That cash helped him survive until conditions improved two years later.

You need a concrete runway figure, perhaps fourteen months in the worst case, and evidence that the major leaks have been stopped. The number should no longer be shrinking every day.

2. Recover the capacity to make decisions

Your judgment may be impaired by the situation you're trying to judge.

In their 2013 study Poverty Impedes Cognitive Function, Mani and colleagues found evidence that financial concerns can consume cognitive resources and affect performance on cognitive tasks. That isn't a claim that intelligence declines permanently, or an explanation for every crisis. The useful idea is a "bandwidth tax": an urgent problem can occupy so much attention that other decisions become harder. Before treating mistakes as evidence of incompetence, examine the pressure under which they were made.

If circumstances allow, set aside two to four weeks in which you postpone major irreversible decisions: a large loan, an impulsive marriage or divorce, quitting in anger, or staking everything on a new business. Restore regular sleep and suitable exercise. At least seven hours of sleep a night is a useful priority; thirty minutes of daily exercise can be a starting point for adjustment, rather than a prescription that fits everyone's health. Remove sources of anxious comparison. Find a steady friend or mentor, with no conflicting interest, who can help you examine the situation.

Stress narrows your field of view. A local failure can begin to feel like a judgment on your whole life; a temporary downturn can look permanent. Making a hurried decision in that state makes it easier to overlook costs and alternatives. Give yourself a chance to describe the problem without having to relive the panic.

During the 2022 sell-off in Hong Kong stocks, a friend managing several hundred million yuan couldn't sleep after repeated heavy falls in his main holdings. He spent his days watching prices and chasing rumors. Trying to recover quickly, he turned over his portfolio more than a dozen times in a month and made the losses worse. I persuaded him to spend ten days in the mountains, away from his trading computer, running and reading history. When he returned and looked at his positions, his reaction was disbelief: "How did I end up owning these stocks? There's no logic to them."

Can you explain your position and its main constraints to an outsider, calmly, in three minutes? And can they understand what you mean? That's a useful sign that some perspective has returned.

3. Separate bad luck, missing skills, and a bad position

"Nothing works for me" is too vague a diagnosis to act on. I find it more useful to separate three kinds of problem, because they require different responses.

An external shock may involve a regulatory change, a recession, an unexpected illness, or a public-health emergency. Acknowledge the loss without treating every part of it as your own fault.

A capability gap calls for learning. You may need better financial management, negotiating skills, emotional regulation, or the ability to use AI tools. Estimate the cost and time required to close that gap.

A poor position calls for reconsidering where you're working: a shrinking industry, an organization with little room to grow, or a circle that drains your energy. More skill may not fix the structure around you.

Write down the problems separately. One of the most expensive mistakes is trying to solve a positioning problem by becoming better at the wrong job. There is little point in competing for a better cabin on a sinking ship. Distinguish the outside constraints you cannot change from the variables you can.

A reader I advised had been a middle manager in traditional private education. After the industry changed, his pay was halved; he worked fourteen-hour days and still faced redundancy. He blamed his management ability and enrolled in an expensive MBA. Our discussion separated the issues. The industry's contraction was an external shock. Remaining in a shrinking business was a positioning problem. His useful skills in course development and community operations needed a new market, perhaps services for older customers or businesses expanding overseas. He dropped the MBA and, three months later, joined a startup selling educational content to older adults. His income soon recovered.

The diagnosis is becoming useful when you can name the main constraint in a sentence or two and write down what evidence would show you've got it wrong.

4. Stop paying for past decisions

Recognizing a bad situation doesn't automatically make it easy to leave. Sunk costs and neglected opportunity costs can keep you there.

The money already lost is only part of the damage. Trying to prove that the original decision was right can consume time, attention, and capital that still have other uses.

Look at the project, investment, job, or relationship you're reluctant to leave. If you were starting today with the resources you now possess, would you choose it again? If the answer is an emphatic no, begin working out how to exit. Keep what you can carry forward: skills, customer trust, and knowledge of an industry. Treat spent money, past titles, and the need to save face as costs already incurred.

Sunk costs don't become recoverable because you make another commitment. What matters for the next decision is what you give up by making it. Sometimes the difficult quality you need is the ability to stop.

Early in my private-market investing career, I backed a smart-hardware project. The founder had a doctorate from a well-known university and strong technical ability, but commercialization was going badly. After the several million yuan invested over two years had run out, he asked for more, saying mass production was one final step away. I couldn't bear to abandon what we'd already put in. I invested again. A year later the project failed anyway. What hurt most was the second investment and another year of work supporting the company. During that period, the capital and attention tied up in it also contributed to my missing an early-stage clean-energy investment that later rose twentyfold.

Make a list of commitments to end, then actually end at least one. The result should be something tangible: time freed, an expense removed, or cash no longer being lost. A written resolution alone doesn't change the constraint.

5. Buy information through small experiments

After stopping the damage, the temptation is to plan a magnificent five-year comeback. But a large commitment made with poor information and few resources is a dangerous way to proceed.

I prefer several small experiments with limited losses and room for an unexpectedly good result. Build three to five around capabilities you already have. Give each a firm loss limit, perhaps 5,000 yuan or two weekends, and a short period in which to learn something: two weeks to a month. The immediate goal is external feedback.

If you're considering a coffee business, for example, you could work weekends in a specialty cafe for two weeks or publish ten pour-over reviews on Xiaohongshu, China's social discovery platform. Does anyone show enough interest to pay for your advice? You can learn that before resigning and committing the money required to open a cafe.

This borrows the logic of an option. A modest amount of money and time buys a chance to discover something useful, with a loss you can survive. You may already have the relevant ability and simply need a setting in which it is valued.

A former student lost his job in property while still paying a mortgage. Instead of borrowing to buy a restaurant franchise or committing blindly to civil-service exams, he examined what he knew: property transactions, writing, and AI tools. He tried three directions with no initial cash outlay: AI lead-generation training for local property agents, articles explaining the risks of court-auctioned homes, and asset-allocation advice for acquaintances. He gave each three weeks. The auction-property articles found an audience; by the fourth piece, more than a dozen readers were asking him about viewings and offering to pay for advice. The other two experiments attracted little interest.

Look for a response you can measure: a payment, a clear willingness to collaborate, or results that exceed a relevant benchmark. "I feel I've learned a lot" is useful personally, but it isn't evidence that the market wants what you're offering.

6. Commit to what works and make it repeatable

Once an experiment produces credible results, continuing to spread your effort evenly can become another form of avoidance.

An investing principle applies here: the gain when you're right has to be considered alongside the loss when you're wrong. As the evidence improves, change the size of the commitment. Then build a routine that doesn't require you to feel inspired every morning.

Cut the experiments that attracted little response and direct more than 70% of your time, energy, and resources toward the promising one. Treat that percentage as a working example, not a universal formula. Translate the aim into small, specific actions with a fixed starting cue. "Build a publication" might become: sit at the desk at eight, write 1,000 Chinese characters, then check the phone.

Progress accumulates when useful effort continues long enough in a productive direction. Repeatedly abandoning that direction can interrupt it. A routine reduces the effort required just to begin, especially when your mood is low. Results can help restore confidence; confidence needn't arrive first.

The former property employee did this after finding readers willing to pay for due diligence on auctioned homes. He stopped the other experiments and made this his full-time focus. To avoid drifting while working alone, he went to a library desk at nine, reviewed three auction-property files and wrote an analysis before noon, then visited two residential developments for checks in the afternoon. He treated this as a minimum routine even after a poor night's sleep. Six months later, he had become known locally in that niche, and his monthly income exceeded his former pay as an executive at a property company.

Check where your working hours go. More than half should now serve the same main direction. On a bad day, can you still do the minimum useful work? And is the work beginning to bring in new customers, opportunities, or income without starting again from zero each time?

7. Build a life that can withstand the next setback

An improvement in income isn't the same as becoming less vulnerable.

After a recovery, it's easy to return to borrowing heavily or relying on one source of income. Without a margin of safety, getting back to even may only mean you survived the last shock.

When cash flow turns positive, consider building a reserve covering twelve to twenty-four months of basic expenses, kept away from high-risk investments. Leave roughly 20% of your schedule uncommitted. These are examples of buffers to consider, rather than requirements everyone can meet immediately. Develop skills you could use elsewhere, such as designing AI workflows, explaining complex ideas, finding customers, or building professional trust. While the memory is still fresh, write down what went wrong, the early warnings you missed, and the mistakes you don't want to repeat.

If you regain your old income but retain the debt, dependence, and blind spots that made the crisis so damaging, the next shock may find you in the same position. The aim is a structure in which an ordinary failure doesn't put the rest of your life at risk.

A factory owner I know nearly went under in 2020 after a major overseas customer defaulted. It took him three years to recover. Instead of following competitors into another debt-funded expansion, he limited any single customer to 20% of revenue, kept enough cash for a year's payroll, and turned a sales team tied to one product into a separate cross-border e-commerce services operation. When exchange-rate volatility and tariff shocks hit the industry last year, his factory's profit fell 30%, but the business held up. He even had room to buy useful equipment from a competitor at a low price.

Imagine the same shock arriving tomorrow. Could you work out your runway in five minutes? Do you have two or three alternatives you could actually use? Those answers say more about your recovery than the income figure alone.

Having somewhere else to go

The sequence matters: stop the losses, recover some perspective, identify the constraint, and stop financing past mistakes. Then try small experiments, commit to a direction with evidence behind it, and build enough reserve to survive another setback.

I don't think there is a final state in which uncertainty disappears. A better position is one in which your set of workable options keeps expanding.

As an investor, the advice I return to for myself and for friends is to resist the all-or-nothing comeback. Stay able to keep playing. Give tomorrow's version of yourself one more viable choice than you have today.

item.title: What Counts as Knowledge?
item.description: AI has made answers cheap. Sound judgment still depends on knowledge—and on whether you can use it when real constraints apply.
item.content:encoded:
I recently met two young people, both fresh out of college.

One had a master's in computer science from a prestigious university, excellent grades, and more practice with algorithm problems than most people I know. The other had an undergraduate degree from an ordinary school, in a field that wasn't even a close match for the job. They interviewed for the same role. The company gave each a small assignment: take a real business need and, in two days, deliver something that actually worked.

The second candidate got the offer.

I've thought about that for a while. A traditional professor might say the first candidate plainly had more knowledge, in a more systematic and rigorous form. That may be true. The company was also right to choose the other person. So what do we mean when we talk about "knowledge"?

My answer is this: real knowledge is the ability to get something done under real constraints and judge whether the result is any good. AI has pushed the price of the part that can be recited or tested on an exam close to zero.

1. Knowing the answer is worth less than it used to be

Start with a simple point that's easy to overlook: knowledge is a kind of product, and its price depends on how scarce it is.

For a long time, knowing something was valuable in itself. You knew how to derive a formula, interpret a regulation, or use a programming language when other people didn't. That knowledge gave you an edge. Much of the university system, from courses and exams to degrees, grew around that scarcity: put knowledge into students' heads, then use exams to check that it stuck.

The cost of getting information has changed. Anything that can be written down, searched, or repeated can now be produced by an AI in seconds, often with a reasonably accurate answer. It doesn't get tired or forget, and the answer may cost nothing. Something that took you four years to memorize can be retrieved by someone else in four seconds.

The thing losing value isn't knowledge itself. It's the kind of knowledge we test by asking people to produce an answer from memory.

The reason is straightforward. An exam typically asks for a standard answer, recalled without outside help. That happens to be a task AI handles well. If a model can ace an exam, the exam is testing something a machine can now supply cheaply. The test hasn't become easier; what it measures has become less scarce.

You can see this in courses that haven't changed in years. Their content may be correct: how to use office software, work with a particular database, or follow a textbook built around one medium. But students finish and find that a chat window can supply much of what they learned. The material hasn't become false. Its value has changed.

That shift affects individuals even more directly than it affects courses. If your main advantage is "I know this," you're in a market where that advantage is getting cheaper. Faster than most people want to admit.

2. Knowledge has to survive delivery

So what hasn't lost value?

Back to the two candidates. What did the second one do? As I understand it, he spent half a day clarifying three points with the business team. He turned a vague request into clear requirements. Then he broke the assignment into smaller tasks and used AI on each one. He ran every piece himself, fixed what failed, and delivered something usable after two days. It wasn't polished, but he knew what was fragile and what still needed work.

The process came down to four abilities: explain the problem, break it down, make something, and test it.

To explain the problem is to turn a vague idea into instructions another person or a machine can act on. It sounds easy. Often it's the hardest part. People struggle to do the work because they haven't yet decided what they want.

To break it down is to divide a large problem into smaller ones, then understand their order and dependencies. That takes a structural understanding of the problem itself.

To make something is to turn an idea into a real object or result. AI is taking on much of the routine work involved.

To test it is to decide whether the result is correct, useful, and good enough to use.

AI is lowering the cost of the first three. The cost of the last one is rising. Once generation becomes cheap, the amount of output grows sharply; someone still has to decide whether each piece can be trusted. If a tool can give you a hundred answers a second, the person who can tell which answer is sound becomes the bottleneck.

I think of this as a scarcity of acceptance: companies increasingly want to know not just "Can you do the work?" but "Can I trust what you deliver enough to use it?" AI may help with the first. The second still depends on your judgment.

That helps explain the gap between someone who can pass a test and someone who can deliver. In the first case, knowledge sits in a person's head; others can't see or verify it. In the second, it appears in something concrete that can run, be checked, and be used. That makes it possible to test and price.

3. The stronger AI gets, the more the fundamentals matter

You might reach this conclusion: if AI can do everything, there's no need to study the basics. Just learn how to direct the tool.

That conclusion is wrong, and risky.

Take a company's financial statements. Feed them to an AI, and within minutes you get a polished write-up. Some of its judgments will be sound; others may only sound plausible. It might mistake a one-time gain for an operating improvement, read an accounting change as real business growth, or describe an industry's competitive structure fluently while missing the constraint that matters.

Someone who understands accounting and the industry may spot the problem at once. Someone who doesn't may simply admire the write-up.

Both people used the same tool and got the same output. The difference was whether they had the grounding to judge it.

Code works the same way. AI can write hundreds of lines in a minute. Whether that code belongs in production depends on whether the person reviewing it understands how the system works, where its boundaries lie, and what could make it unsafe. If you don't, you're handing a client something you can't assess.

That's why I say acceptance is becoming scarce, and why it depends on solid knowledge of the field. The two ideas are sides of one change: knowledge that can be copied cheaply is losing value; knowledge that lets you judge the copy is gaining it.

The difference is between knowing an answer and understanding a problem. Someone else can supply an answer. Understanding can't be handed over so easily. It means knowing why the problem is hard, where mistakes tend to occur, and how an answer that looks right might fail. You get that through sustained, systematic study, not a few rounds in a chat window.

AI amplifies the judgment you already have. With sound judgment, it can extend your reach. Without it, you may make mistakes faster, and make them more convincingly.

That's why I find the phrase "mastering AI" a little misleading. What you master is a field or a skill. AI is a lever you use to do that work. A longer lever is useless without a fulcrum.

4. Knowledge has a half-life

If foundational knowledge matters, should we try to learn everything? Of course not. Time is limited, so we need to decide what deserves it.

I find it useful to think of knowledge in three layers, each with a different half-life.

The outer layer is tools: how to prompt a particular model, call a framework's interface, or combine features in a product. It changes quickly. A best practice from six months ago may already be obsolete. Learn what you need when you need it; don't build your whole education around it.

The middle layer is method: how to define a vague problem, break a large one into parts, design a test, and get closer to a goal through iteration. This lasts much longer. A strong engineer from twenty years ago and a strong engineer today still share these habits.

The inner layer is the field itself: basic economics, how financial assets are priced, the mechanics and systems thinking behind engineering, and statistical inference. These foundations rarely expire. They're also what make sound evaluation possible.

Once you see the layers, the trade-off becomes clearer. Spend most of your time on tools and you're chasing the fastest-moving target. By the time you catch it, it may have changed. Learn tools without methods or a field, and each technology shift can wash away another part of your advantage.

For educators, that means we can't simply chase the newest tools. A framework taught today may be old technology in three years. Methods and fundamentals deserve more of the time because students can use them for life and adapt faster when the tools change.

That doesn't mean ignoring tools. Courses need a way to stay current, so students encounter living practice rather than a decade-old textbook. The materials should change; the underlying structure should hold.

The same question applies to your own learning: how much time do you spend on tools, and how much on methods and the field you work in? If nearly all of it goes to the first layer, the return on your effort may be low.

5. What you test matters more than what you cover

Here's one more point, and the one I think is easiest to miss: what someone learns depends more on how their learning is tested than on the content alone.

People put effort where it will be measured. If the test is an exam, they memorize, practice questions, and work out what the examiner likes. If the test is a real deliverable, they have to ask what problem it should solve, how to solve it, and what it takes to make it work.

The same material, tested in different ways, can produce very different people.

That's why I'm skeptical of reforms that simply add AI material to a course. If students hear a few lectures on AI but still take a conventional final exam, they'll learn the exam material: the names of model architectures, perhaps a few prompting tricks. They may still have no idea how to use the technology to get something done at work.

Change the content but keep the test, and the result is unlikely to change.

Assessment matters for another reason: it determines how quickly people get feedback. An exam gives a score, often long after the work, without showing exactly where the student went wrong. A deliverable gives immediate feedback. Does it run? Does the user find it useful? You can try it and see. That density of feedback is a major source of learning.

There's a qualification. Education can't be judged entirely by whether a company wants the result. Some things students learn at university help them understand the world, form judgments, and become thoughtful people. Those things may not turn into a deliverable right away. Reducing education to job training would be a loss.

That doesn't contradict my point. If education is meant to cultivate understanding and judgment, it should be less dependent on testing what a machine can reproduce from memory. Real understanding means being able to apply an idea in a new setting, explain it, make a judgment, and produce something. A real deliverable may be a better test of that than recall alone.

Back to the two candidates

I want to return to the two young people at the beginning.

I don't think the first candidate was unqualified. Quite the opposite: he had a strong foundation. If he changed how he tested his own learning, he could catch up quickly. The second candidate had gaps too. Without filling them, he'd soon hit a ceiling.

For young people, my advice is concrete: stop measuring yourself by how much you've studied. Pick a small, real goal. Make something, hand it over, and let someone use it. You'll discover which parts you understand and which only feel familiar. That discovery can teach you more than a hundred exam papers.

If you follow investing and AI, take an inventory of what you know. Which parts are "exam knowledge," and which can survive delivery? Knowing what a price-to-earnings ratio means is exam knowledge. Taking a particular company and explaining why its earnings are, or aren't, durable, then being willing to put real money behind that judgment, is closer to delivery.

AI can help with the first. The second has to be yours. This week, choose one thing you've wanted to understand and turn it into something you can show someone else: an analysis, a small tool, or an essay someone could challenge.

item.title: What Makes an Investment Bubble?
item.description: What future does the price require, can new investment earn its cost of capital, and who is financing the expansion? Three questions for judging how fragile a boom has become.
item.content:encoded:
What the price is asking you to believe

When is an industry merely doing well? When is it getting expensive, overheating, or caught in a dangerous bubble? I want a way to distinguish those conditions that gives us more than another adjective.

An asset price makes a claim about the future. The buyer is paying on the assumption that future cash flows will justify the outlay. To examine that claim, I ask whether the required future can occur, whether the capital being spent to produce it can earn an adequate return, and who will bear the loss if it doesn't. A large price increase doesn't answer those questions. A high valuation might be justified. And dismissing the technology doesn't help: technologies associated with past bubbles often became useful parts of the economy.

That gives me three layers to examine. Valuation asks what profits, revenue, and end demand the market price requires, and how those requirements compare with historical experience. Investment asks whether new capital can earn more than its cost and whether revenue comes from paying end customers. Financing asks whether the spending is funded by operating cash flow or outside money, and who might be forced to sell if conditions deteriorate.

The layers matter because the damage can spread. A valuation problem hurts the holders of the asset. Poor investment returns can hurt the industry and its suppliers. Fragile financing can pass the loss to creditors and the wider financial system.

My four categories describe an accumulation of those vulnerabilities. In a healthy boom, demand and earnings are growing and the three layers look reasonably sound. In a stretched market, the price requires something close to an optimistic outcome, although the underlying investment and financing still look viable. In an overheated market, capital is also pouring into projects whose marginal returns approach or fall below their cost, creating excess capacity. A speculative frenzy adds vulnerable financing: leverage, outside funding, or circular arrangements help prices and capital flows push each other higher, while valuation discipline is discarded.

The size of the rally isn't what determines the category.

The unit of analysis matters too. By an investment theme, I mean capital drawn together by a common narrative, such as AI. Chips, electricity, cloud infrastructure, models, and applications can occupy different stages at the same time. Each needs its own examination; a single score for "AI" conceals too much.

1. A rally is a clue, not a diagnosis

The strongest objection comes from Eugene Fama's challenge: if bubbles could be identified in advance, why wouldn't prices already have adjusted? I think the objection needs to be taken seriously, but it doesn't settle every question about risk.

In their 2019 paper Bubbles for Fama, Robin Greenwood, Andrei Shleifer, and Yang You distinguish average returns from crash risk. A sharp industry rally need not predict unusually low subsequent average returns. It can nevertheless predict a higher probability of a crash. Those are different results, and confusing them changes the conclusion.

The study also finds that volatility, turnover, issuance, and the path of the rally help distinguish subsequent outcomes. Price increases contain information, but they don't make every rally a bubble. I want to examine the accompanying conditions.

There is another serious objection to a purely valuation-based diagnosis. In their model published in 2009, Lubos Pastor and Pietro Veronesi show how technological change can generate prices that look like bubbles afterward even when investors behave rationally. Uncertainty and learning about adoption matter. Expensive alone isn't a definition of irrationality.

2. The same return can conceal different risks

My framework concentrates on three ingredients: prices that outrun fundamentals, price increases that generate further buying, and fragile financing.

Overvaluation alone is a weak basis for declaring a bubble because it can overlook growth and uncertainty. Fragile credit isn't a necessary condition for every bubble either. The latter two ingredients help explain how a boom feeds on itself and how costly a reversal might become.

Each judgment should answer a question we can investigate. Two assets can both double in price while presenting very different risks. In one, earnings and cash flows may support the move. In the other, borrowed money may be keeping the process going.

3. Work backward from the market value

Start with the market capitalization and work backward. What profit does it require? What revenue would produce that profit? How much of the relevant industry's spending would have to become end demand for the product? Compare the required growth and its duration with what similar businesses have achieved.

An expensive asset may grow into its valuation. A price that requires an implausible economic outcome presents a different problem. The task is to find out how much room there is between a demanding assumption and one with no credible path to delivery.

Comparing an index's earnings yield with Treasury yields can help start the inquiry. But that spread isn't a complete measure of the equity risk premium. Growth, the earnings measure, and risk still need to be considered.

4. Spending ahead of revenue can be sensible

During infrastructure development, investment commonly arrives before the revenue it is meant to support. Railways, electricity networks, and cloud computing have all required that sequence. A large gap between spending and current revenue doesn't by itself establish a bubble.

Ask instead whether each additional dollar can earn a return above the cost of capital over the asset's useful life. Useful life is crucial. Railway infrastructure can last decades. Servers and accelerators can need replacement much sooner, so they have less time to earn back the initial investment.

Then examine who pays. Is revenue coming from end customers, purchases among related industry participants, investor subsidies, or supplier financing? If a significant share of orders comes from customers financed by the vendor or its investors, those sales deserve closer scrutiny. During the 1999–2000 telecom expansion, equipment suppliers including Cisco and Lucent financed customers who used that money to purchase equipment. Sales looked healthier than the demand that could survive without that funding. When customers ran short of cash, orders disappeared too.

Supply also responds. Attractive returns draw new capacity. Constraints in power or advanced packaging can delay excess supply, but their removal can allow a substantial amount of capacity to arrive together.

5. Find out where the money comes from

The same investment program can have very different consequences depending on how it is financed. If a company pays from operating cash flow, shareholders bear much of the direct investment loss. Debt, off-balance-sheet arrangements, and private credit can transmit losses to creditors and financial institutions.

Capital flows can also move prices more than intuition suggests. Xavier Gabaix and Ralph Koijen's inelastic markets hypothesis estimates a market-value increase of roughly $5 for each $1 invested in the aggregate stock market, with the estimate depending on the sample and method. The point is the potential size of the price response to flows, not a multiplier to apply mechanically to every trade. Outflows deserve the same attention as inflows.

Narrow market breadth is another clue that needs interpretation. Profits themselves may be concentrated, so a rally driven by a small group of companies isn't enough to establish a bubble. Compare their share of index market value with their share of index profits. A wide gap can reveal how much depends on those few companies fulfilling expectations.

6. Watch the financing conditions

A rising price strengthens the story, draws in money, and helps raise the price again. That is the kind of feedback Soros describes as reflexivity.

We tend to imagine that a bubble ends when investors recognize it. Often the immediate trigger is more practical: buyers run out of room, funding costs rise, orders disappoint, or new supply arrives. The underlying technology doesn't have to be useless for the financing to stop working.

For someone monitoring a theme, that makes funding conditions at least as important as the next technological announcement.

7. Credit changes who pays for the collapse

The consequences depend on how the boom was funded. In their 2015 study Leveraged Bubbles, Oscar Jorda, Moritz Schularick, and Alan Taylor examine seventeen advanced economies over roughly 140 years. Bubbles accompanied by credit booms tend to produce more severe economic damage when they collapse, with deeper recessions and slower recoveries. Equity booms without comparable credit expansion can have smaller costs.

Calling something a bubble therefore leaves a crucial question unanswered: who will bear the loss this time?

8. Put the questions to the financial statements

The three layers can be applied to the AI industry, but a research framework should be distinguished from a live market assessment. The calculations below are illustrative assumptions, not a claim about today's prices or yields.

Suppose an index is reaching new highs while fewer than half of its constituents are above their 200-day moving averages. Is a small group carrying the index? Compare those companies' shares of market value and earnings. Examine the capital drawn into the common theme instead of treating the entire market as one trade.

For an interest-rate example, assume a ten-year Treasury yield of 5.3%. Its reciprocal is roughly nineteen. That provides a crude reference for comparing the Treasury yield with an equity earnings yield; it isn't a maximum reasonable price-to-earnings ratio. Earnings yield isn't the shareholder's realized total return either. If the companies driving the rally trade above that reference, the case for owning them relies more heavily on future growth. Whether valuations are stretched still depends on earnings quality, the durability of growth, concentration, and financing. Nineteen times earnings cannot settle the question.

When a price already discounts a great deal of progress, examine the next two layers through two groups of financial indicators.

The first concerns incremental returns relative to the cost of capital. The 5.3% in the example is a risk-free benchmark. A company's cost of capital also reflects risk and its financing structure. Companies rarely report a separate return on AI projects, so we need imperfect proxies. One is the relationship between cloud revenue growth and growth in depreciation and amortization. Depreciation growing ahead of revenue during construction isn't unusual. Revenue growth slowing over several quarters while depreciation accelerates deserves investigation. It isn't, by itself, a calculation of project returns. Check remaining performance obligations and customer concentration too. Are customers paying from operating revenue, external funding, or money invested by their suppliers?

The second group concerns capital expenditure relative to operating cash flow and how any gap is funded. A ratio persistently near or above 100% calls for examining cash reserves, asset sales, and outside financing. Look at bond issuance, debt balances, interest burdens, and lease commitments that haven't yet commenced. Read those measures alongside solvency: a strong balance sheet can provide substantial room. Private credit, joint ventures, and project financing may require assembling disclosures from the statements, their notes, and separate financing announcements.

I can specify what would change my assessment before those results arrive. If the gap between revenue and depreciation growth keeps worsening while the capital-spending shortfall becomes increasingly debt-funded, I'd move the risk assessment from stretched toward overheated. Either development alone would call for closer observation rather than an immediate verdict. Conversely, covering capital spending from operating cash flow reduces dependence on outside finance. It doesn't rule out impairment, excess capacity, or a valuation loss.

9. A bubble diagnosis isn't a trading signal

Identifying a bubble doesn't mean you can make money from it. A bubble can persist. Mistaking a durable expansion for one also carries a cost: staying entirely in cash while earnings and cash flows grow can be expensive.

I translate these judgments into exposure decisions rather than automatic buy or sell signals. In a healthy or stretched market, participation requires understanding how much future success is already paid for. In an overheated market, reduce exposure and examine which businesses can cover their investment needs from cash flow. In a speculative frenzy, don't build a plan that depends on selling at the exact top.

The cloud buildout in the 2010s is a counterexample worth considering. My reading is that much of the expansion was closer to a boom than a credit-fueled bubble because large companies financed substantial investment from their own operating cash flows. That structure can reduce credit contagion without implying that the entire industry experienced no credit events. Readers should still examine the evidence for themselves.

For any investment theme, I would finish with three questions:

  1. How demanding is the future required by the price, compared with historical growth outcomes?
  2. Can the new capital earn more than its cost, and does the revenue come from end customers?
  3. Was the money earned or borrowed, and who could be forced to sell if the assumptions fail?

The more those answers deteriorate together, the more fragile the boom becomes.

These are my research judgments, not investment recommendations.

item.title: Peter Thiel on Substance over Status
item.description: What Thiel's arguments about competition, credentials, and career choices can teach young people—and where his advice needs qualification.
item.content:encoded:
A question for graduation season

Every graduation season brings a familiar set of questions: Should I join a big company or take a civil-service exam? Go to graduate school or join an investment bank? Stay in a major city or move back home? The details change, but the question underneath is often the same: Which path looks respectable, feels secure, and earns other people's approval?

Peter Thiel is a useful person to read against that instinct. He co-founded PayPal and founded Founders Fund. Zero to One grew out of an entrepreneurship course he taught at Stanford in 2012; his student Blake Masters turned his notes into the book. Thiel's own résumé looks like the model elite track: Stanford as an undergraduate, then Stanford Law. Yet he has spent years questioning the paths that credentials and convention make seem inevitable.

Two qualifications before I begin. "Substance" and "status" are my shorthand for themes in Thiel's work; he did not present a complete doctrine under those two labels. I'll mark my own extensions as I go. I've also relied on my recollection of some chapter references and interview details. Where I'm unsure, I've left the detail out. Check the book or original interview before quoting any of it.

1. Fierce competition may be a sign you chose the wrong contest

First, it helps to be precise about what Thiel means by competition. In the textbook model of perfect competition, companies earn only a normal return in long-run equilibrium; economic profit approaches zero. One of Zero to One's central claims is that good companies tend to escape that condition, while those trapped in it spend much of their energy just staying alive. Around the book's publication, Thiel adapted one of its arguments for The Wall Street Journal under the title "Competition Is for Losers." The headline was sharper than the article.

I'm more interested in another point from chapter four, which draws on René Girard's theory of mimetic desire. We often learn what to want by watching other people. If everyone is competing for something, it starts to look valuable. The harder the rivalry, the more each side watches the other—and the easier it is to forget why the contest began. Thiel uses PayPal's early fight with X.com as an example. Both companies paid a high price for the rivalry; the contest ended only when they merged.

For a young person choosing a job, school, or title, the test is plain: Did you decide this prize was worth pursuing, or does it look worthwhile because everyone around you wants it? People often treat a crowded race as proof that the prize is valuable. Thiel's warning runs in the other direction: a crowd may mean everyone is reacting to the same signals.

That doesn't make competition bad in every setting. Exams, sports, and markets all use it to sort ability and spur improvement. As I read Thiel, his objection is to making "winning" the goal. If you can't say what the win leaves you with, it may be an empty victory.

2. A credential is a signal, not the thing itself

Thiel has spoken about failing to get a clerkship with the U.S. Supreme Court. My reading is that he was pointing to the pull of a prestigious job: much of its appeal may come from the fact that everyone wants it, not from whether the work suits you. Check the book for the exact details.

In a 2011 interview with TechCrunch's Sarah Lacy, he argued that American higher education had become a bubble. In broad terms, tuition kept rising as families came to believe that a student without an elite degree had no future. Education was being bought as insurance, but it was also a status race. Around the same period, Thiel launched the Thiel Fellowship, offering $100,000 each to young people who would leave school for two years to work on a project of their own.

The strongest part of this argument is the distinction between being certified and getting something done. In the classic economic model of signaling, a degree may help an employer judge someone whose productivity they don't yet know; the credential need not make that person more productive. An elite diploma answers, "How will other people read me?" Ability answers, "What can I make or do?" The two may be closely connected early in a career. Over time, what you've actually done matters more than where you studied.

There's a counterpoint worth keeping. The Thiel Fellowship is itself a form of elite selection. Many recipients were already unusually capable, so critics are right to ask whether it replaces one status system with another. An elite school offers more than a label, too: training, peers, and access to opportunities. Those benefits shouldn't be waved away. As I understand him, Thiel is questioning the impulse to treat the label as the goal, not the value of learning.

3. The "safe" path can hide a long-term bet

Chapter six of Zero to One sorts attitudes toward the future along two axes: pessimistic or optimistic, definite or indefinite. Thiel's target is "indefinite optimism": the belief that things will get better, without a concrete account of how or a plan to get there. In his view, finance, consulting, and law became default destinations for elite graduates partly because they preserve options. You can move in several directions later; you don't have to decide now what you want to build. The chapter's title, "You Are Not a Lottery Ticket," makes a related point: outcomes aren't just luck. You can plan and act to shape them.

There's an important distinction here. Keeping options open can be sensible, especially for someone carrying student debt or trying to get on stable footing. Thiel's narrower target is someone who has choices but keeps choosing not to choose because commitment feels uncomfortable.

Here I'm extending his argument. A "safe" path may protect your current income and standing while leaving your position ten years from now uncertain. If every job is chosen for where it might lead next, you can spend the years best suited to deep work accumulating a broadly acceptable résumé instead of a hard-to-replace ability. The risk is easy to miss because each individual year looks fine.

Imagine two people of the same age. One moves through three respectable jobs in five years. The other spends those five years working on the same narrow problem. The first has the more polished résumé. The second may have a judgment about that problem no one else can easily match. Which one is safer depends on whether you're looking at year one or year ten.

4. Substance begins with a truth others may reject

Thiel likes to ask candidates a question: What important truth do very few people agree with you on? It appears in the first chapter of Zero to One. He has also said it's hard to answer well. Most of our views come from school and the people around us; few are ideas we've worked out for ourselves.

He describes the shape of a good answer roughly this way: most people believe one thing; reality points the other way. What's easy to miss is that he wants a truth, not disagreement for its own sake. Contradicting the crowd just to look original is another way of following it.

Chapter eight, "Secrets," takes up a related idea: every good business is built around something others haven't noticed, whether it comes from nature or from people. Thiel pushes back against the belief that everything worth discovering has already been found and all that remains is to improve what's on the existing map.

That's where substance and status meet. Status is granted by other people and has to be seen. Substance is something you've figured out; it remains true even if no one has noticed yet. My own view is that if you can't name an independent judgment you've made in your field, much of your competitive edge may come from your title or platform. Change platforms, and that advantage may go with it.

One practical caution: an independent view still needs testing. Disagreeing with most people doesn't make you right. Start small. Write down a judgment about a specific question, the evidence behind it, and what would change your mind. Come back six months later and check.

5. Create value; don't just fight over a fixed share

Chapter three contrasts two figures from the book: in 2012, U.S. airlines earned an average of 37 cents per passenger, while Google's profit margin was about 21 percent. Thiel's explanation is that intense competition had pushed airline prices close to costs, while Google faced little competition in search, giving it room to set prices and invest over time.

His use of "monopoly" doesn't mean predatory conduct. He means a business has made something with no close substitute for the time being—the "creative monopoly" he describes in the book. His advice is to start in a small, specific market, become difficult to replace there, then expand. PayPal initially focused on power sellers on eBay.

Applied to a career, this is my extension: much of the anxiety at work comes from occupying a role with many substitutes, where you have to be more diligent or more visible than your colleagues just to hold your place. That's a fight over a fixed slice. A value-creation question is different: What use is my work to someone else? If I weren't here, could another person easily fill the gap?

Thiel's monopoly argument is contested. Antitrust authorities and many economists wouldn't accept monopoly as a general measure of success, and I have reservations too. Some monopoly profits come from creating something valuable; others come from using barriers to keep others out. Their consequences for social welfare are very different. What I take from Thiel is the method: find out whether what you make has a substitute before asking how to make it bigger.

6. Don't turn a life into a diversified index fund

Chapter seven is about power laws. In venture capital, the best investment in a successful fund can return more than all the others combined; Thiel draws on his own fund's experience. The implication is that a few decisions can determine most of the outcome, so the quality of a decision matters more than the number of decisions.

He carries the idea over to life: don't make your life a diversified index fund; find a few things worth pursuing deeply. I remember that extension appearing in the second half of the chapter. Check the book for the precise wording.

My reading is that a few choices matter especially much for a young person: which field to enter, whom to work with, and which problem to spend years on. Their consequences can differ enormously. By comparison, another internship or credential often adds little at the margin. In that sense, depth can matter more than breadth.

But there's a condition. A fund can make many bets and survive a few failures if it hits a handful of winners. Most people get only a few major bets in a lifetime, and a bad one can be hard to recover from. So don't copy the fund mechanically. Keep the cost of failure within what you can bear: earn enough to support yourself, then put some time and money into focused experiments. And remember that the stories we hear about people who bet right are selected survivors.

Thiel is speaking from a position of considerable resources. That belongs in the calculation when we read him.

7. Join a team without joining its status race

PayPal's early team is Thiel's main example in chapter ten, "The Mechanics of Mafia." He wanted each person to own a distinct responsibility and be judged on it. His reasoning was that many internal conflicts arise when responsibilities overlap: if two people do the same job, they can end up fighting over credit, resources, or importance.

The book doesn't make a separate argument about titles and rankings. What follows is my extension of his idea.

A title is cheap status currency inside a company. It costs no cash and satisfies the desire for recognition. When titles become the main concern, attention shifts from doing the work to being seen doing it. Clear responsibilities help move evaluation from "Who are you?" to "How well did you handle what you owned?" The second question is harder to perform for an audience.

I'd suggest two things when joining a team. Ask what you're responsible for and how that work will be judged; don't let "well-rounded development" become a substitute for a clear role. Then look at the relationship between promotion and value created. If advancement depends mostly on tenure or connections, build results in your own area that others can verify.

There are limits. Large companies need levels and reporting lines to coordinate and motivate people; they can't simply do away with hierarchy. The point here is where you put your own attention.

After reading Thiel, my overall impression is that he isn't arguing against hard work or elite schools. He's arguing against spending yourself on a goal you haven't examined, using other people's approval as the measure. His ideas also come from a privileged position and carry a survivor's perspective. They're worth considering, with that discount applied.

Three questions to ask yourself

  1. If no one could see or praise the position I'm pursuing, would I still spend the same time trying to get it?
  2. Ten years from now, what will I have that no one can take away and few people can easily replace?
  3. In my field, what do I believe that most of my peers don't? What evidence do I have?

This essay draws on Peter Thiel's Zero to One and related interviews and course material. It is not investment advice.

item.title: Li Lu on AI: The Risk of Treating a Machine as a God
item.description: AI can transform the economy and still disappoint investors. Li Lu's Columbia discussion offers a way to think about price, China, geopolitics, and what compounds over a lifetime.
item.content:encoded:
What struck me about Li Lu's recent discussion at Columbia was how he connected AI, the United States, China, and markets. Technology changes the world, capital follows it, and politics reshapes its boundaries. Yet long-term investment returns still depend on value, price, costs, competitive advantage, and how rationally people behave. AI may be the largest variable in this cycle without overturning the basic rules of investing. The more dramatic the technology and the more excited the market, the more those unglamorous rules deserve our attention.

Li Lu covered value investing, AI, China's economy, US–China relations, the global political order, and compounding over a lifetime. Taken together, these subjects left me asking what changes with a changing world, and what holds.

1. The danger of pricing AI as a god

Over the past few years, a familiar story about AI has grown beyond the idea of an increasingly capable tool. It now imagines something approaching a god of our own making.

As a tool, AI can help people perform more and more tasks. The more ambitious story says it will eventually solve problems we cannot solve ourselves, transforming economic growth, productivity, wealth creation, and the structure of society.

The distance between those two claims is much greater than it first appears.

Li Lu repeatedly returned to that distinction. He acknowledged AI's extraordinary capabilities and its potential to become one of history's most important technologies. But he was wary of drawing a straight line from today's systems to artificial general intelligence, then superintelligence, and finally a world in which intelligence faces almost no limits. Development, in his account, involves more than making models increasingly capable. Costs, energy, capital, human involvement, and social acceptance impose constraints of their own.

For investors, one implication deserves attention: society's willingness to tolerate a technology's risks may limit how far it can go.

What a system can do and what people will allow it to do are separate questions.

Consider autonomous driving. A system might be statistically safer than human drivers and still face public resistance when it makes a mistake. The stakes are higher still in medicine, finance, the courts, and the military. In such settings, technical feasibility is only the beginning. Who takes responsibility when something goes wrong? Will the public accept the risk? Will regulators permit it? Are people willing to surrender the final decision?

AI's practical limits therefore extend beyond the capabilities of its models.

Engineering determines what a technology can do. Economics, institutions, and human attitudes help determine whether it will actually be used.

"Will AI reach AGI?" doesn't tell me enough as an investor. Even if AI acquires a particular capability, who will pay for it? Who will bear the risk? How much existing spending can it replace? How much additional value can it create?

Those questions bring the discussion back from technological awe to economics.

None of this rules out productivity gains far beyond what we see today. If AI substantially lowers the marginal cost of knowledge work, it could become an exceptionally powerful general-purpose technology.

A technology can create enormous value for society without delivering enormous returns to everyone who invests in it.

Electricity, cars, and the internet transformed the world. Capital committed to those industries early on did not automatically earn excess returns commensurate with their social contribution.

The investment question, then, is: how much of AI's future is already in the price?

When valuations assume almost unlimited potential, the risk is that even a remarkably successful AI industry may fall short of the success investors have already paid for.

2. Real progress can still produce a boom and bust

One of Li Lu's more consequential observations was that AI's development could involve several rounds of boom and bust, rather than a single uninterrupted expansion.

To me, the point is less a forecast of the next bubble than a broader economic lesson:

A technological revolution that continually consumes capital, energy, infrastructure, and organizational resources will have a capital cycle as well as a development curve.

AI looks like software, but much of the industry increasingly resembles a capital-intensive business.

Training models requires computing resources; running them requires more. Data centers need land, electricity, and networks. Chip production entails enormous capital expenditure. Infrastructure investment continues throughout the supply chain.

This is a long way from a pure software business with marginal costs approaching zero.

Once markets become convinced that a technology has a vast future, money pours in. Investment buys more computing capacity, better models, and wider adoption. Those advances appear to vindicate the original optimism, drawing in further capital.

That feedback loop cannot run indefinitely.

Eventually, investors need to know how much actual cash flow these investments will generate.

If cash generation fails to keep pace with investment, the cycle turns. Returns on capital weaken, valuations contract, projects fail, excess capacity emerges, and markets reprice the industry.

This helps explain why technological revolutions can pass through successive booms, busts, and renewed growth.

An AI bubble, if there is one, would not by itself mean the technology is a fraud.

Some of the most dangerous bubbles form around technologies capable of changing how we live and work.

A worthless technology has difficulty sustaining widespread conviction. A technology that genuinely changes the world gives speculation something far more durable to feed on.

The internet and railways changed the world; both also produced bubbles. AI may follow a similar course.

In discussing the AI market, Li Lu returned to valuation and a useful long-term anchor: stock-market returns cannot indefinitely outstrip the earning power of businesses and the growth capacity of the economy.

That is an easily neglected part of value investing.

Valuation ultimately comes down to arithmetic, however impressive the technology.

An outstanding company in a remarkable industry still has to answer three questions: how much future cash can it generate, how much will reach shareholders, and how much must an investor pay today?

Technology can increase the cash those businesses produce. The price you pay determines how much of that success becomes your return.

I would therefore spend less time debating whether AI deserves the word "bubble" and more time asking:

Have I already paid for ten or twenty years of exceptional success?

If so, AI could change the world and still leave the investment disappointing.

3. Look beyond the future everyone is buying

This may have been one of the most practically useful points in Li Lu's discussion.

When capital concentrates in AI, it need not make the entire market expensive. Some assets attract intense enthusiasm while others become cheap through lack of attention.

Li Lu described a deeply divided market and suggested that such disparities could improve the opportunity set for rational investors.

The idea fits naturally with value investing.

Markets do not reliably assign the right price to every asset.

Much of the time, they allocate attention instead.

Capital pursues fashionable industries, analysts cover fashionable companies, and the media follows fashionable stories. Entrepreneurs respond to what investors want to fund. The busiest areas accumulate more information, discussion, and higher valuations. Elsewhere, businesses may receive less research, attract less competition for their shares, and be mispriced.

Such opportunities can be hard to act on even when we see them. Investing rationally often demands more of our temperament than our intelligence.

A severalfold rise in an AI stock can make you feel you have missed your chance. Years of stagnant prices in an established business can make you conclude it has no future.

Rising prices generate reasons to be bullish; falling prices generate reasons to be bearish.

Investors then read a rally as evidence that the market has discovered value, and a decline as evidence that it has uncovered a problem.

A value investor has to return to the business:

What has actually changed in the company since its share price moved?

When the change in business value is much smaller than the change in price, the discrepancy may be an opportunity.

An overlooked asset is not necessarily a bargain.

Some companies deserve the market's neglect. Declining industries, deteriorating business models, falling returns on capital, and poor management can all turn a low valuation into a value trap.

The task is more demanding than buying whatever happens to be out of fashion:

Find assets whose fundamentals are better than their prices imply, but which are being overlooked as attention concentrates elsewhere.

That is a promising place to direct research in the current market.

The more capital AI attracts, the more deliberately investors should widen their field of view.

There's no need to oppose AI on principle. Attention has an opportunity cost in every market.

When everyone looks in the same direction, better prospective returns may lie elsewhere.

4. China's economy has two stories running at once

The most useful part of Li Lu's discussion of China, in my reading, was a way of looking at the economy that went beyond declaring it either troubled or full of opportunity:

Two distinct layers of the Chinese economy are operating at the same time.

One is under pressure from the property adjustment, household balance sheets, and weak consumer confidence.

The other involves industrial upgrading, technological progress, extensive supply chains, growing self-reliance, and stronger global competitiveness.

It is a mistake to collapse them into a single story.

Looking only at the first can make China seem devoid of long-term opportunity. Looking only at the second can obscure the real costs of the property correction, household balance-sheet repair, and insufficient demand.
