If restructuring cash payments precede the savings, the timing would become less favorable. Assessing how much less favorable requires the actual schedule of payments and savings. All else equal, an equal amount of cash arriving later has a lower present value than one arriving sooner.

The central point remains: cutting costs may help a business survive, but it cannot, by itself, make consumers want the brand again. That requires renewed strength in products, culture, and distribution: a turn in revenue, rather than an attractive EBIT presentation alone.

5. Take the counterarguments seriously, then define the conditions

There is a case for continuing to hold, and it deserves consideration.

First: Jefferies maintained a Buy rating, although its target had been cut from $75 to $60.

According to October 2 reporting on the Jefferies note, the analyst continued to recognize improvements in North America and performance products, while acknowledging pressure in Greater China, Jordan, and Sportswear. A $60 target was still substantially above the roughly $32 price discussed here, but an analyst target is a judgment, not a promised return. Another constructive argument is that November's investor day and subsequent guidance could clarify the turnaround. The possibility that current expectations already absorb the bad news deserves testing; a new CFO alone does not establish that guidance has deliberately been set low to create later upside surprises.

Second: North America grew 2%.

That suggests the brand had not collapsed in its largest mature market, and that its core products retained appeal. It is a real positive that should not be ignored.

Third: short positions were crowded.

In its September 29, 2026 report, S3 Partners put shares sold short at more than 87 million, with its short-interest measure rising from below 3% to above 7%. Those are the provider's figures at that date, rather than live data. A crowded short position can become fuel for a rebound if better-than-expected news triggers covering.

This is where reflexivity enters the picture. A share price can affect fundamentals as well as reflect them. A falling price may weaken equity incentives, make financing or acquisitions more expensive, and erode partners' confidence, adding pressure to operations. A positive surprise may help restore confidence. Crowded shorts contain both information about sentiment and the potential for a sharp reversal.

My purpose is to give a long-term holding an evidence framework: under what conditions does keeping it remain the best use of capital?

  • First, revenue stabilizes before we declare success on profit. Watch whether sales declines narrow, especially across several quarters in Greater China, rather than relying on EBIT alone.
  • Second, the source of margin improvement can be verified. Does it reflect product mix and pricing power, or contraction in promotions and distribution? The first can be healthy; the second may spend future strength.
  • Third, November's investor day provides a testable route to recovery: dates and measures, including the timing of savings and the limits of restructuring charges, rather than slogans.
  • Fourth, evidence supports the rebalancing of distribution. With Nike Direct down 8% and wholesale down 1%, the chosen direction must ultimately earn its case in the data.

The more these conditions are met, the stronger the case for continuing to hold. The fewer that are met, the more the position resembles an emotional option on the Nike you remember.

This is not personal investment advice or a prediction of Nike's share price. An evidence framework gives you a standard written before new information arrives, rather than an emotional explanation assembled afterward.

6. Your own version of Nike

Employees and entrepreneurs can face a similar problem: living off an asset built in earlier years while investing too little in its future.

Your career, skills, professional reputation, and relationships can compound. The judgment you have developed over ten years, and what colleagues believe about your work, form a valuable personal brand. It can accumulate strength, or lose it.

What does harvesting that asset look like?

  • Earning a high salary from skills developed a decade ago, while your current income statement still looks strong.
  • Repeating comfortable work efficiently, posting good annual results, but never extending what you are capable of doing.
  • Treating your reputation as something to cash in whenever a short-term benefit appears.

These choices can produce a high apparent margin because little is being reinvested. But eventually the revenue side responds: the industry changes, technology changes, and so does the value of what you offer.

AI brings this pressure into sharper view. A skill that once supported someone for twenty years may now have a much shorter useful life.

Reallocating human capital becomes increasingly necessary. That means:

  • Devoting time to capabilities that can keep compounding: judgment, integration across fields, effective collaboration with AI, and trust that has been earned.
  • Avoiding continued investment in depreciating skills merely because they are familiar.

This returns us to two abilities a long-term approach requires: the ability to continue, and the ability to stop. Most people train only the first, treating persistence as virtue and stopping as failure. But sunk costs should not determine the future. Opportunity cost and the prospects for compounding should.

Taking the long term seriously means sustaining productive compounding while ending allocations that no longer support it.

A checklist for yourself

Here is a framework you can apply to investments, careers, and businesses. Ask yourself every six months:

  1. If I were starting from zero today, would I choose this allocation again? If not, why am I keeping it?
  2. Where does my apparent profit come from: new compounding, or consumption of assets built in the past?
  3. Is my revenue base expanding or contracting? Look beyond comforting numbers to the source of growth.
  4. Is there a Greater China in my own life: an ability or field showing a warning on the scale of a 26% decline, while I reassure myself with other measures?
  5. Have I written an evidence framework for continuing? Are the conditions for staying and reallocating explicit?
  6. Am I waiting for a reversal, or working to create a turn? Waiting alone is not a strategy; action is.

Nike might become desirable again. It might not. Time and execution will answer that question about the company. Your question is where to put the next unit of capital, the next hour, and the next year.

Do not keep harvesting your own brand until there is nothing left to grow.

Source note: Company data come from Nike's announcements; market prices, expectations, and analyst views refer to reports from October 1–2, 2026. Short-position figures come from S3 Partners' September 29 report. The gross-profit calculation in section four is illustrative, not a company forecast. This essay expresses a personal view and is not investment advice.

item.title: Everyone wants GPUs. Why are CPUs running short?
item.description: As AI moves from producing answers to completing tasks, its bottlenecks shift. Follow an agent's workflow to understand rising CPU demand—and what would make the shortage last.
item.content:encoded:
CPUs are becoming increasingly prominent on AI infrastructure shopping lists.

In late September, reports from industry channels suggested that 2027 production of AMD's sixth-generation EPYC processor, Venice, was already booked, with orders spilling into 2028. AMD has not officially confirmed the claim. Even so, pressure on server CPU supply is attracting attention. Reported supply constraints

Intel has also signaled a shortage. According to coverage of Splunk .conf26, its CEO said the company could currently meet only about half of customers' CPU demand. That figure cannot be translated directly into a global supply gap. Intel's formal second-quarter disclosure, however, confirmed that demand exceeded available supply and that industry-wide shortages of critical components, including substrates and memory, were expected to persist into 2027. Coverage of the remarks; Intel quarterly filing

Generating an answer and completing a task make very different demands on computing infrastructure.

When AI starts executing tasks on people's behalf, the work falling to CPUs grows too.

1. A faster GPU still has to wait for everything else

Ask a coding agent to fix a bug, and it must do much more than generate a few lines of code.

It needs to read the project, propose a solution, and edit files. Then it must start an environment, compile the code, and run tests. If a test fails, it sends the error back to the model, makes another change, and tries again.

Model computation relies primarily on GPUs; code execution and much of the tool work rely on CPUs. A task moves back and forth between these stages. Delivery speed depends on the entire workflow.

Consider a simplified time budget. Suppose a task originally takes 100 seconds: 90 seconds for model computation and 10 seconds for other steps that cannot, for now, be accelerated.

StageBefore the GPU upgradeAfter model computation becomes 10× faster
Model computation90 seconds9 seconds
Other steps10 seconds10 seconds
Total time100 seconds19 seconds

The GPU's portion becomes ten times faster, but the whole task speeds up by only about 5.3 times. Steps that originally accounted for one-tenth of the time now take more than half of it.

That is the constraint described by Amdahl's law: for a fixed-size task, the benefit of accelerating one part is limited by the work that remains. The numbers illustrate the mechanism; they are not measurements of an average real-world agent. NVIDIA CUDA best practices guide

A more visible bottleneck does not, by itself, mean CPU demand must rise. If the same number of tasks is processed each day, a GPU upgrade might simply shorten waiting times. Network latency, disk access, and sequential dependencies cannot necessarily be resolved by adding CPUs either.

What drives procurement is the next step: companies use the freed-up GPU capacity to run more tasks at once. More code needs compiling, more tests need running, and more execution environments need starting. Only then does the total amount of CPU work increase.

2. One person asks; a team of agents gets to work

In a conversation with a chatbot, people usually pause to read the answer, think, and ask another question. Human reading and judgment place a limit on the frequency of requests.

Given a goal, an agent can run repeated cycles of planning, tool use, checking, and retrying on its own. A single bug-fix request might trigger dozens of tests. A research task might involve numerous web visits and database queries. Several agents can also work on different subtasks simultaneously.

The user assigns one job; behind the scenes, many rounds of computation and tool use may already be underway.

This expansion remains constrained by budgets, permissions, and success rates. Companies will keep agents running only when the value of the completed work covers the costs of model calls, execution, and review. Once that condition is met, CPU load is no longer determined solely by how often people ask questions. It also depends on how many attempts and execution environments each task requires.

Training agents adds to these demands. To learn to write code and use tools, models must repeatedly attempt tasks and verify the results. Many of those tools and environments run on CPUs.

When NVIDIA introduced the Vera CPU in March 2026, it described a rack with 256 CPUs supporting more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments. Under the design disclosed by the company, these resources serve execution and training at scale. Vera CPU announcement

TrendForce also expects CPU-to-GPU ratios in agent deployments to move from the 1:4–1:8 range associated with traditional large-model workloads toward 1:1–1:2. The projection applies to specific deployment scenarios. It reflects the need to rebalance hardware as execution work increases. TrendForce analysis

3. Orders can rise quickly. Production capacity cannot.

Changing demand is colliding with the time required to expand supply.

AMD has announced the production ramp of Venice on TSMC's 2-nanometer process. The next generation of CPUs also needs advanced manufacturing capacity. Wafer fabrication is only the first step: packaging, substrates, memory, and complete server systems must follow. AMD production-ramp announcement

A shortage at any stage can prevent a finished chip from becoming a usable server on schedule. Intel's disclosures about substrate and memory constraints show that the supply pressure extends beyond processors themselves. Intel quarterly filing

More execution environments also need more memory capacity and bandwidth, as well as power and cooling. Buying more CPUs therefore adds orders across the supporting infrastructure.

Companies can increase software concurrency quickly. Hardware suppliers must add equipment, improve yields, coordinate components, and validate platforms. Procurement plans and usable computing capacity are separated by a lead time that cannot simply be skipped.

How long that takes depends on the particular bottleneck. Adjustments to existing production lines, new-product ramps, and supplier expansion can all ease the pressure. Each must be judged by what is actually delivered.

4. The same data center may need more CPUs

The scale of CPU demand also depends on what a data center runs.

In a March 2026 presentation, Arm estimated about 30 million CPU cores per gigawatt for a traditional AI data center, potentially rising to 120 million cores in an agentic configuration. This is a vendor's estimate for specific scenarios, including CPU resources adjacent to accelerators—not a universal standard for every data center. Arm presentation, pages 3–4

Those two endpoints allow a simple sensitivity analysis.

Suppose newly commissioned AI capacity is G gigawatts, and the share using a CPU-intensive agentic configuration is p. With linear interpolation, the additional core requirement can be written as:

Additional CPU cores = G × (30 million + 90 million × p)

For a hypothetical 10 gigawatts of new capacity:

Share with CPU-intensive agentic configurationsCPU cores requiredEquivalent at 128 cores per processor
10%390 millionAbout 3.05 million processors
30%570 millionAbout 4.45 million processors
60%840 millionAbout 6.56 million processors

The 10-gigawatt capacity assumption, configuration shares, linear interpolation, and conversion at 128 cores per processor are illustrative. They are not an annual forecast or an industry-average configuration. Nor are cores from different architectures fully interchangeable.

Even with identical additions to capacity, a change in workloads alone could more than double CPU requirements.

Estimating a global shortfall would also require accounting for general-purpose server replacement, upgrades to existing AI facilities, and equipment reuse, then comparing that demand with each supplier's effective output. Public data is not yet sufficient to complete that calculation.

Whether new products ramping in 2027 can ease the shortage therefore depends on how much CPU demand per data center rises as supply expands. A judgment about future balance must consider capacity growth, workload mix, and software efficiency together.

5. A lasting shortage needs real work for AI to do

Strong bookings must eventually be supported by actual use.

Customers worried about availability may buy early or place duplicate orders. Longer lead times strengthen the incentive to stockpile. If real workloads fail to keep pace, today's bookings may become tomorrow's inventory and cancellations.

Software efficiency can change demand too. Reducing unsuccessful retries, reusing execution environments, and combining queries can lower the CPU resources needed to finish a task. Slower data-center construction would also reduce new purchases.

Three signals are worth watching:

  • Are delivery times for comparable server CPUs continuing to lengthen?
  • How much revenue growth comes from shipments, and how much from a richer product mix or higher prices?
  • Do cloud providers' construction and procurement plans become commissioned capacity and sustained workloads?

Volume and price are particularly easy to confuse. Intel's second-quarter server average selling price rose 48% year over year, while shipments rose 9%. The company attributed the price increase primarily to a higher-end product mix. Rapid revenue growth need not mean equally rapid growth in CPU units sold, and cannot be converted directly into a market shortfall. Intel quarterly filing

The renewed attention to CPUs reflects AI's expanding scope. Once a model can propose more solutions, a system still has to execute code, call tools, read data, and check results. What companies actually buy is a completed job, delivered by all these stages together.

Whether the CPU shortage lasts ultimately depends on whether the work companies will pay AI to do grows faster than the infrastructure required to deliver it.

item.title: Build a thesis you can challenge
item.description: Understand how a business creates value, then identify the evidence that could change your mind.
item.content:encoded:
Before asking where a price will go, ask what you own and why its value might change. A useful investment thesis starts with the business, not with a target price.

Start with the engine.

Describe who pays the company, what they pay for, and what has to happen for revenue to become cash. Separate growth in volume from changes in price or product mix.

Write the counterargument.

Choose the strongest explanation for why your thesis could be wrong. A competitor could lower prices, a customer leave, or growth require more capital than you expected.

Name the next evidence.

Record the operating indicator you expect to change, when you expect to see it, and what result would make you reconsider. The point is a decision you can revisit, not a prediction you have to defend.

item.title: Give AI a job, not a wish list
item.description: Evaluate a tool against a real task, including the time it takes to check and repair its output.
item.content:encoded:
A new model is interesting. A repeatable improvement in your work is useful. Start the evaluation with one task you already do, and a clear definition of a good result.

Choose one bounded task.

Try structuring source notes, reviewing a draft, or classifying documents. Keep sensitive information out of a service until you understand its access and data controls.

Measure the whole workflow.

Include the time spent writing instructions, checking output, and correcting mistakes. A fast first draft that requires extensive repair may not save time.

Keep a human checkpoint.

Decide which claims need sources and which actions require your approval. Save a small set of examples so the same workflow can be tested again when tools change.

item.title: The nature of consumption
item.description: Change the label on the same bottle of wine, and it tastes different. For anyone who sells a service, everything before delivery is the evidence a client uses to judge you.
item.content:encoded:
In 2008, researchers at Caltech and Stanford conducted an experiment in which they asked around twenty participants to lie inside an MRI scanner while wine was dripped into their mouths through a small tube. The participants were told they were tasting several wines at different price points. In fact, one wine was presented twice: once as a $10 bottle and once as a $90 bottle. The participants generally rated the $90 wine as better. That part was hardly surprising. Everyone has been influenced by a price tag at some point. What was surprising was what the scans revealed: when drinking the wine labeled "$90," the brain region directly associated with pleasure was indeed more active. In other words, the participants weren't just being polite or pretending to know more about wine than they did. They genuinely enjoyed it more.

Change the label on the same bottle of wine, and the taste changes. Every time I think about this experiment, it makes me a little uncomfortable, because it exposes a distinction we have grown accustomed to making: the product is real, the feeling is subjective; quality comes from the former, while the latter belongs to the bag of marketing tricks. But the experiment tells a different story. The feeling isn't something layered on top of the product. It is directly involved in determining whether the wine tastes good in the first place. Consumers pay for products and services. That's the part we can see on the surface. What they ultimately receive, and remember, is a feeling.

I. Before Paying, Clients Can Judge You Only by How You Make Them Feel

People who sell services tend to resist this idea. I've encountered plenty of highly capable professionals—lawyers, designers, consultants, and home renovation contractors—who share a simple conviction: do good work, and clients will recognize it. Websites, company profiles, and document formatting are just packaging, nice extras that add a little polish. There's something admirable about this belief. The problem is that it overlooks a crucial time lag. The quality of a service only becomes apparent after it has been delivered. Hire a lawyer, and you won't know how good they are until the case is over. Hire a renovation company, and you may have to wait two or three years to find out whether the walls will crack. Yet payment comes first, and the contract is signed first. Between paying and seeing the results, clients have to make a judgment. And the only evidence available to them is what you put in front of them before delivery: a website, a company profile, a WeChat reply, a quote, or a proposal.

So, what professionals dismiss as "packaging" isn't packaging at all from the client's perspective. It's evidence—and often the only evidence they have. Economics has a concept called signaling. When buyers and sellers have unequal information, the more capable party needs to send a signal that an incapable one would find too costly to imitate, making their true quality recognizable. A doctor's white coat, a law firm's solid-wood reception desk, Apple's long wooden tables in its stores—none of these things serves much practical function. What they offer is a kind of collateral: I've invested in this, and I'm here for the long haul, not just to make a quick buck and leave. Conversely, a service provider whose website still uses an outdated template, whose quotes rely on Word's default fonts, or whose proposals contain typos may be genuinely excellent at the work itself. But before paying, clients have no way of knowing that. People who complain that clients don't recognize quality often haven't even put that quality on display.

II. Everything Before Delivery Is Already Part of the Delivery

These pre-delivery details affect more than whether you get chosen. A client's evaluation of a service doesn't begin on the day the work starts. It begins with the very first interaction. How long it takes you to reply to the first WeChat message, whether your proposal follows a clear line of reasoning, whether your quote breaks down the items in an understandable way—all of this happens before delivery, yet it has already shaped the expectations in the client's mind. When the work is finally delivered, the client isn't experiencing your service on a blank slate. They're comparing it against the expectations you've already established. With the same quality of work, a rigorous first impression makes the client think, "Just as I expected." A casual, careless first impression puts them on the lookout for flaws, magnifying every minor issue into confirmation of what they suspected all along.

Psychologist Daniel Kahneman developed the peak-end rule, which holds that our memories of an experience aren't based on its average quality. They depend primarily on its most intense moment and how it ends. IKEA has applied this principle thoroughly. You might spend two hours shopping, finding products, waiting in line, and carrying boxes—a fairly exhausting experience. Yet the one-yuan ice cream cone at the exit can rewrite the memory of the entire trip as "pretty good." And what determines whether someone comes back or recommends you to a friend is precisely that memory, not the experience itself. Apple's attention to packaging follows the same logic. Those few seconds when the lid slowly lifts off a box are said to have been refined through repeated testing. The difference between a company that tests even the unboxing experience and one that believes a good product is all that matters isn't really about aesthetics. People who sell services often think their business begins only after a contract is signed. In the client's mind, your business started long ago. You're just the last person to realize it.

III. What People Buy Is the Person They Become After Buying

The previous sections explained where feelings come from. This one asks what those feelings contain. Consumers rarely care deeply about the details of a product. Specifications, craftsmanship, ingredient lists—most people glance at them and move on. What they really care about is something else: What kind of life will I lead after buying this? What kind of person will I be in the eyes of others? You can buy yoga pants with the same basic functionality as Lululemon's for a few dozen yuan. The premium buys an image: discipline, a comfortable margin in life, and a sense of responsibility for one's own body. Arc'teryx's rise in popularity in China over recent years has relatively little to do with an increase in the number of people who actually go mountaineering. It has become a marker of identity. Wear it, and people in certain circles will recognize you as one of their own. Pop Mart makes the point even more directly. The plastic figurine is often put on a shelf not long after being unboxed. What people are really paying for is those few seconds of uncertainty before the box is opened.

Anthropologist Clifford Geertz once wrote, in essence, that human beings are animals suspended in webs of significance they themselves have spun. In today's consumer society, that statement needs one word changed. The web is still there, but we are no longer the ones weaving it. Much of it is woven by businesses. Perhaps the most successful example is the diamond. Before De Beers launched "A Diamond Is Forever" in 1947, diamonds had no inherent connection to marriage. A piece of carbon, a line of advertising, and suddenly the two were bound together by the idea of "eternal love." Decades later, diamonds had become the default choice for marriage proposals in many places. Nothing about the diamond's physical properties had changed. A thread had simply been tied between a stone and a desire that already existed in the human heart.

At this point, many people would naturally reach a conclusion: if consumers buy feelings, and feelings can be manufactured, then it doesn't matter whether those feelings are real. I disagree. Return to the wine experiment at the beginning. The pleasure the participants experienced was not fake. Their brains were responding in a very real way. Feelings aren't a veneer laid over reality. They are part of reality itself. A piece of clothing that makes you stand taller when walking down the street, or a service that puts you at ease from beginning to end—these are genuine changes that take place. To call feelings fake is to underestimate their power.

IV. But Feelings Cannot Sustain Themselves

We need to turn a corner here, or the argument can easily slide into another dangerous conclusion: all I need to do is make the packaging look good. No. Feelings create expectations; products fulfill them. They are two consecutive links in the same chain, not alternatives to each other. Feelings determine whether you get chosen the first time. The product determines whether you get chosen again. If the first link breaks, no one will discover how good the work behind it is. If the second link breaks, the better you make the first impression, the greater the debt you accumulate.

Chicecream, a Chinese ice cream brand, is a classic example. From the beginning, it positioned itself as a premium product, emphasizing ingredients, craftsmanship, and the sophistication of a single ice cream bar. This narrative worked in the early days. But when its products appeared in ordinary convenience-store freezers, consumers would casually pick up a bar and discover the price only at checkout. At that moment, the feeling wasn't luxury. It was being ripped off. In the summer of 2022, the Chinese term "ice cream assassin" spread rapidly to describe expensive ice creams that ambushed unsuspecting buyers at checkout. To some extent, it was an act of retaliation. The higher the expectations, the greater the anger when they went unmet—far out of proportion to what a single ice cream bar should warrant.

Luckin Coffee took a different path. In its early days, subsidies and relentless marketing drew people into its stores. That was the emotional layer. What eventually established the brand was the development of products people repeatedly came back for, such as its coconut latte. That was the fulfillment layer. Both have to work. Packaging is a promise, and promises must be kept.

V. What Can Service Providers Actually Do?

My advice is to start with something simple, even tedious: map every point of contact between the moment a client first hears about you and the moment they finally pay. Where do they hear about you? What do they see first? What appears when they click through? How do they get in touch? How long does it take you to respond? What does the first document they receive look like? How do you present your quote? Once you've listed everything, ask yourself one question about each item: What is this telling the client? Most people who complete this exercise discover that half their touchpoints are effectively saying, "We just do this casually." And the clients have received every one of those signals.

As you build this list, consistency matters more than polish. Every touchpoint should convey the same feeling. If you're selling rigor, your quote cannot contain typos. If you're selling ease, your website shouldn't sound like a stiff corporate brochure. Mix incompatible styles here and there, and clients won't perceive two sets of strengths. They'll simply think, "I can't tell who you are." Another task is to turn abstract capabilities into tangible evidence. The statement "We're highly professional" conveys almost no information. Everyone says it. Replace it with "Here's our project workflow document" or "Here's a post-project review from a similar engagement," and the client has something concrete to evaluate. Capabilities themselves are invisible. The evidence they leave behind can be seen.

VI. Back to That Glass of Wine

Those participants weren't stupid. Faced with limited information, they made a judgment using the only available clue, and their bodies responded accordingly. Most consumers behave the same way. Saying that consumers buy feelings doesn't mean they're superficial. They can judge you only by what you put in front of them. If you hand over a sloppy quote, they'll conclude that you're sloppy. Given the information available to them, that judgment is perfectly reasonable. Rather than complain that clients can't recognize your expertise, make your expertise recognizable.

item.title: Investing requires thinking one level up
item.description: The people who bought PetroChina in 2007 and Moutai in 2014 were not answering the same question when they placed their orders. Look one level higher at a time: time, probability, structure, where returns come from, and yourself.
item.content:encoded:
On November 5, 2007, PetroChina's A-shares began trading on the Shanghai Stock Exchange at 48.62 yuan. People were lining up outside brokerage offices that day. The media called it "Asia's most profitable company," and buying its stock was presented as a way to share in the nation's energy lifeblood. A year later, the share price had fallen to 9.7 yuan. For most of the decade and a half that followed, it hovered between 7 and 10 yuan. Those who bought on the first day and never quite found the courage to sell eventually became famous as the punchline of investment jokes.

Around the same time, in January 2014, someone else bought Kweichow Moutai at around 118 yuan a share. The mood was almost the exact opposite of what it had been when PetroChina went public. The plasticizer scandal was still fresh, the government's Eight-Point Regulation had been introduced, group-purchasing channels had largely dried up, and a wave of distributors were selling off inventory at a loss. Moutai's price-to-earnings ratio had fallen to just over eight. Bearish views on liquor were the mainstream opinion, not a minority position. Brokerage research reports were full of phrases such as "channel collapse" and "prices inverted."

The difference between these two groups is usually explained in terms of who had the better eye for stocks. I don't think that's it. The real difference was that, at the moment they placed their orders, they were answering entirely different questions. Those buying PetroChina were asking, "Is this a good, big, profitable company?" Those buying Moutai were asking, "At this price, has the market already priced in the bad news likely to come over the next few years?" The second question operates at a higher level than the first. No matter how hard you work to answer the first, you cannot arrive at an answer to the second. This is what I mean by thinking one level up.

Let's start with time. The phrase "long-term investing" has been repeated so often that it has almost lost its meaning, and it is frequently misunderstood. The PetroChina investors held on for more than a decade, longer than most people who claim to be long-term investors. Holding for a long time did not improve their results. Time is on your side only if the underlying business is likely to improve over time, or at least not deteriorate. When that condition does not hold, time is not your friend but an accelerant. It accelerates decline just as readily as growth.

In 2014, Moutai's earnings were indeed falling, but several fundamental features of the business remained unchanged: customers paid before receiving their goods, the company did not need to commit large amounts of capital to expand, and it could raise prices without having to negotiate with distributors. The disruption in its distribution channels was cyclical; these characteristics were structural. Cycles pass. Structure endures. PetroChina was the opposite. It had no control over oil-price cycles, its exploration and refining operations consumed enormous amounts of capital expenditure every year, and the proportion of its earnings that ultimately reached minority shareholders in the secondary market had not changed. Hold it for ten years, and it would still be the same business. The sequence matters: first determine whether the business is likely to remain viable and profitable ten years from now; only then can time work in your favor. Reverse that sequence, and you are using time to gamble on something you have never properly understood.

The next level up is probability. Most people approach investing as if it were a series of true-or-false questions: Will the price rise or fall? Is this good or bad? Should I buy or not? Get the answer right and you make money; get it wrong and you lose. This approach feels intuitive, but it is highly inefficient. In the first half of 2015, many people around me predicted that a bull market was coming, and they were right. The Shanghai Composite Index rose from 2,000 to 5,178. There was nothing wrong with that call. But after June, several of those people had used margin financing at a 1:5 leverage ratio. During the successive limit-down sessions, they could not sell. By the time their accounts were forcibly liquidated, the index was still above 4,000. Their prediction was right. They were wiped out.

There is a reverse example, too. Someone began saying in early 2018 that Tencent was too expensive. That year, Tencent fell from HK$476 to HK$251, and the call was right. From 2019 to early 2021, however, it climbed all the way to HK$775, and the person was wrong for more than two consecutive years. In 2022, it fell to HK$198, and the call was right again. Over seven years, the calls alternated between right and wrong, roughly a fifty-fifty record by count. But suppose this person had invested a fixed amount every month throughout those seven years, never used leverage, and never liquidated the position during any downturn. The final result would have had far less to do with the accuracy of their predictions than most people imagine. Three other factors would have mattered far more: how much they wagered each time, whether they could survive being wrong, and whether they still had capital available when they were right. A casino never tries to predict whether your next hand will win or lose. It cares about only two things: the maximum bet and the number of hands played. Shifting your attention from "Am I right?" to "Is my way of betting positive or negative in expectation over the long run?" is the second step up in thinking.

The third level is structure. Changchun High-Tech provides a classic example. Before 2021, its human growth hormone business had delivered several consecutive years of strong growth. Institutional investors crowded into the stock, and brokerage research reports were overwhelmingly positive. After May 2021, news of centralized government procurement began to emerge, while doubts about eligible indications and market penetration also grew. The share price subsequently fell more than 70% from its peak. You could argue that investors had not researched the company deeply enough, but I see it differently. The company's revenue was heavily concentrated in a single product, and the pricing power for that product rested in the hands of policymakers. You could read the annual reports until you had memorized them and interview every distributor, yet you still would not know when a policy document would arrive or exactly what it would say. This is not a research problem. It is a structural problem, and structural problems can only be solved structurally. You can own the stock, but you cannot let it determine whether you survive as an investor. The same principle applies to heavily investing in a company whose revenue depends on a single major customer, or putting most of your money into the best stock in an entire sector. Neither is simply a question of whether you understand the business. Even when you understand it, the risk remains. Many people misunderstand portfolio construction as diversification into mediocrity. A portfolio is not designed to dilute returns. It is designed to ensure that no single mistaken judgment can force you out of the game. Being able to stay at the table after getting something wrong matters far more than getting this particular decision right.

The fourth level is to ask yourself a particularly simple question: If I make money on this investment, who, exactly, is paying me? There are only four possibilities: the company pays me dividends; the company's profits grow, increasing my share of those profits; the market becomes willing to pay a higher price for the same amount of profit; or the next person is willing to buy the shares from me at a higher price. The first three ways of making money involve earning alongside the business. The fourth involves making money out of someone else's pocket. The difficulty differs by an order of magnitude.

LeEco's stock reached a high of 179 yuan in 2015. The people buying it were not necessarily blind to the fact that the company was unprofitable. Many knew perfectly well what was going on. They were betting on the fourth possibility: that someone else would take the baton from them. In 2020, the stock was delisted, and during the delisting period it fell as low as 0.18 yuan. Tencent was a different case. From 2018 to 2021, its profits generally kept growing, yet its share price first fell from HK$476 to HK$251, then climbed to HK$775, before dropping back to HK$198. Most of the fluctuations in between were not driven by changes in profit, but by changes in the valuation multiple the market was willing to assign. If you think you are making money from the second source when you are actually making it from the third, you have no idea when you should get out. In recent years, people have started buying PetroChina again, but the rationale has changed. They are no longer buying for growth, but for dividend yield. The same company can generate returns in entirely different ways. Understanding that is far more useful than arguing over whether it is a good company.

The final level is one that almost nobody accounts for: yourself. In 2015, brokerage research analysts heavily invested in brokerage stocks. On the surface, their reasoning was, "I understand this industry better than anyone." In reality, they had tied both their salaries and their investment portfolios to the same variable. In the second half of that year, industry bonuses were cut, and the stocks were also halved in value. The situation was even more extreme in 2021. People working in the private education sector held shares in New Oriental and TAL Education. When the government's "double reduction" policy was announced in July, Chinese education stocks listed in the United States lost 70% to 90% of their value in a single month. Many people lost both their jobs and their investment portfolios. Your salary is one source of beta; your portfolio is another. They should not depend on the same underlying factor. A real estate employee borrowing heavily to buy a third property, or a bank employee putting all their money into bank stocks, is making the same fundamental mistake.

There is another level beneath that: when will you need the money you are investing? Money needed for a down payment within three years and money that will not be touched for twenty years are fundamentally different, yet people often invest both according to the same logic. Many investors do not lose money primarily because they chose the wrong asset. They lose because they need the money at the worst point in the market and are forced to sell at the bottom. That is why the first line of a truly complete portfolio sheet should not be a stock ticker, but information about you: what you do for a living, how stable your income is, how much debt you owe, and what major expenses you expect over the next three years. These factors determine how much risk you can bear. The market does not care how much you can bear.

You do not need to memorize all these levels. In practice, there are really only three things worth doing. First, before placing an order, write down three lines: how long you intend to hold the investment, where your returns will come from, and the maximum you could lose if you are wrong. If you cannot write down any one of them, do not buy yet. This may seem simplistic, but it can prevent more than half of impulsive trades. Second, shift your attention from "Has the price gone up?" to "How much have I wagered?" Your judgments will always sometimes be right and sometimes wrong, but your position size is the one thing you can fully control. The same investment thesis means two entirely different things when you allocate 10% of your portfolio versus when you invest everything with leverage. Third, once a year, put your income, debts, future expenses, and investment holdings on the same sheet and review them together. Most people have never done this. Once they do, they discover that they are far less diversified than they imagined.

Thinking one level up does not guarantee that you will make money this time. What it does is keep one mistaken judgment from driving you out of the market permanently. Those who survive in the market for a long time have never done so simply by making more accurate predictions. They survive because, when they do not fully understand what is happening, their losses are still limited.

This article reflects my personal thoughts. The companies mentioned are used solely to illustrate the points discussed and do not constitute investment advice. All investment decisions carry risk, and you are responsible for your own decisions.

item.title: How a person's understanding of value grows
item.description: Some judgments show how much you understand only after you have used them in your own life. A single choice of apartment shows how experience fills in the costs you left out.
item.content:encoded:
A saying often attributed to Charlie Munger circulates online: "There are no true value investors before the age of forty." The original source of this quotation has yet to be verified, but it raises a question worth exploring: What does a person have to experience to develop a genuine understanding of value? (Chinese-language example)

I take "forty" as a reminder rather than a hard rule: some judgments only reveal how much we truly understand them after we have put them to use in our own lives. We may learn early on that time is precious, health matters, and reliability is a virtue. Yet we may still have little sense of how much weight to give these things when making concrete decisions.

Renting an apartment can bring this difference into focus. Imagine someone just starting their career, choosing between two apartments. One costs 1,000 yuan less per month but adds two hours to the daily commute. The other is more expensive but close to the office. After doing the math, the person sees that the cheaper apartment will save 12,000 yuan a year and chooses it. In the calculations they make at the time, the money saved is the easiest benefit to see.

Once they move in, however, the time spent commuting begins to acquire a concrete cost. They want to cook a proper meal, but by the time they get home, it is too late. They want to learn something new, but after a shower, all they want to do is lie down. On weekends, they still need to catch up on the sleep they missed during the week. Those two hours, which once existed only as a distance on a map, have become time each day in which nothing else can be planned.

Experience supplies the costs their first judgment left out. At first, they were comparing two rental prices. Only later did they realize that every day, they were paying the difference in time and energy. The words "time is precious" finally came to represent a tangible loss.

When renting again, they will make a more complete calculation: How much energy will remain after the commute? How much hardship can the money saved actually relieve? Will paying more rent put pressure on their daily life? They may choose to move closer, or they may continue living farther away. The decision itself need not change, but now they understand what they are exchanging for what.

Each person's understanding of value grows out of these different circumstances. Someone who urgently needs to save money may be willing to put up with a long commute. Someone who must care for family in the evenings may place greater value on getting home on time. The same two hours represent different opportunities and responsibilities to different people. When someone makes a choice different from yours, it may simply be because they are bearing costs you do not have to bear.

At first, it is easy to adopt ready-made standards. A high salary means a good job; knowing many people means having a broad network; a packed schedule means a productive day. These standards are convenient, but they often leave out one basic question: What must you give up to obtain these things, and is the exchange worth it to you?

Life gradually brings the omitted factors into view. If a high-paying job consistently eats into your rest and time with loved ones, its value needs to be reassessed. If a friend reliably follows through on every promise, "dependable" becomes more than a compliment. It becomes a reason to entrust that person with things that matter. Value begins to shape concrete trade-offs.

Judgments about investments must also stand up to reality, but the value of a business has its own operational foundations. No matter how much you like a company, you still need to examine whether it can earn money consistently, whether it can turn its earnings into cash, and whether its purchase price is reasonable. Experience shows you risks you missed before, but personal feelings cannot substitute for these fundamentals. What life decisions and investment judgments have in common is that you must bear the consequences of your own understanding.

Experience can also breed prejudice. You move closer to work, encounter a terrible landlord, and conclude that cheap apartments are the only reliable option. You lose money on an investment and decide that every opportunity is a scam. A person can go through the same kind of experience many times and still do nothing more than repeat the same interpretation. For experience to become sound judgment, you must also distinguish between the parts of an outcome caused by your own choices and those attributable to chance.

Forty, then, can only be a figure of speech. Young people can uncover flaws in their judgment early through reading, observation, and small-scale experiments. Older people may spend their entire lives refusing to revise their answers. We do not have to personally experience every wrong turn, but we do need to understand seriously how other people's experiences differ from, and resemble, our own circumstances.

Developing your own sense of value can begin with a concrete review of a past decision: What did you want at the time? What did you actually pay? Which costs did you fail to account for? How will you adjust your approach next time? An experience begins to become understanding only when it can change a future choice.

With such a standard of value, when everyone around you praises an opportunity, you have a basis for deciding whether to accept it. You know what it can bring you, and you know what it will take away. Others can tell you how good an opportunity is, but in the end, the final reckoning must be settled against the reality of your own life.

item.title: Respect the bubble
item.description: Between judging that valuations are too high and judging when prices will fall lie shifts in capital, interests, and expectations. An industry that adjusts on its own makes short sellers pay for the wait.
item.content:encoded:
The gap between recognizing that an industry is overvalued and knowing when it will fall is filled by changes in capital, interests, and expectations. That gap is where short sellers are most likely to pay a price. Especially when an industry has already attracted enormous amounts of capital and built an extensive network of vested interests, any prediction of an imminent collapse must account for how its participants will respond to adversity.

The network of interests surrounding AI has grown far beyond a handful of model companies. In its March 2026 funding announcement, OpenAI listed participants including Amazon, Nvidia, and Microsoft. Anthropic's May 2026 funding announcement named Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix as strategic infrastructure partners. Capital investment and computing-power purchases are linking different parts of the industry. OpenAI funding announcement Anthropic funding announcement

These connections mean that a model company's progress toward commercialization affects investor returns, cloud providers' revenue, and equipment suppliers' orders. Under pressure from slower-than-expected revenue realization, participants have incentives to raise additional capital, adjust their products, and seek new use cases for which customers will pay. As long as further investment is still considered worthwhile and funding remains available, the industry has room to keep experimenting.

That is why a bearish view on AI must consider how the industry will respond to difficulties. Following the existing pricing model to the conclusion that "token prices fall, revenue comes under pressure, and valuations collapse" risks overlooking the room companies have to adapt. They can shift what they sell from model calls to the delivery of an entire piece of work. Intercom's Fin already charges by what it defines as an "outcome," showing that this approach has entered commercial practice. Intercom pricing

A different pricing model can change the benchmark customers use to compare prices. Suppose a task previously cost a business $50 in labor, while the inference cost for AI to complete it is $1. If the AI can deliver reliably and actually reduce the business's expenses, the service provider may have an opportunity to charge $5 or $10. The customer cares about the total cost of getting the job done. Inference cost is only one component.

Whether this works depends on whether the product genuinely delivers the promised outcome. Human review, system integration, and error handling all incur costs. Saving an hour of work does not necessarily translate into one fewer hour of wages paid. Switching from token-based pricing to task-based pricing does not automatically confer pricing power. The new model only makes commercial sense when customers recognize the savings, are willing to keep paying, and the provider can retain a profit amid competition.

Yet the market's observation period may already have lengthened before the results are fully tested. The debate, previously centered on the price per call and revenue growth, now has new questions to contend with: Can tasks be completed consistently? Are customers expanding their usage? Do pilot projects lead to renewals? These questions require new data. A single round of product adjustments may be enough to buy companies more time to secure financing and validate their business models.

Time matters especially in a technology industry that is still evolving. If task success rates improve and delivery costs fall during that period, applications that were previously uneconomical may become viable. New customer demand may then generate revenue to fund the next round of investment. Financing can therefore change the eventual outcome. Expectations that investors consider impossible to realize today may gain some support in the future as products and costs evolve.

Short sellers are up against an industry that actively adapts. Business models, product boundaries, and sources of funding can all change. Even when the profitability problems identified at the outset are real, they may not trigger a decline along the expected path or within the expected timeframe.

This ability to adapt is still constrained by cash flow. Expanding the addressable market from software budgets to white-collar wages does not directly generate more revenue. The tasks that can be automated, the cost savings that can actually be realized, and the share ultimately captured by service providers all determine the market that can be monetized. If only the valuation framework expands while customer spending and operating efficiency fail to improve, the extra time may simply allow losses and capacity pressures to accumulate.

The interests of industry participants will not remain aligned forever, either. Cloud providers want to reduce computing costs. Chip suppliers want to preserve their margins. Model companies compete for customers, while enterprise customers demand lower prices. Shared expectations of growth can sustain cooperation, but conflicts over how profits are distributed can also drive substitution and competition. The AI cycle can continue without every company in the value chain maintaining its current revenue and valuation.

Respecting the bubble means tracking the conditions that sustain valuations: who can still obtain funding, who is improving actual returns, and who is merely postponing problems. For short sellers, a change in pricing models alone is not enough to invalidate a bearish thesis. But when that change genuinely extends a company's financing runway and improves customers' willingness to pay, the original catalysts for a decline and the cost of maintaining the position deserve to be reassessed.

Every trade must ultimately stand the test of the price path it takes. How much time an industry can buy and how long investors can afford to wait will both change the outcome. Seeing the exaggeration in market expectations is only part of the task; one must also understand the forces sustaining those expectations. The market does not spare anyone the cost of waiting simply because they spotted the problem early.
